Terry Gerton Over there at Enabled Intelligence, you’ve spent a good amount of time actually building a very interesting workforce, optimizing neurodivergent talent. What led you to think that this particular group might have advantages for you in the kind of AI and data analysis work your company performs?

Peter Kant Sure. What we were looking for that we are the front end of AI model development. So anytime an AI software gets built or AI technology gets built, the first thing that happens to train that AI is you need people to create the data that it learns from. So people have to teach every AI, whether that’s, you know, Reddit or Facebook information or newspaper information, teaching a large language models to folks using CAPTCHA, if you’ve ever used CAPTCH and said, you know, put a box around, tell me where all the traffic lights are. That data is used to teach autonomous vehicles like Waymo, that’s data labeling. So there’s people at the front end of all AI technology. And those people with AI, especially for government technology or for critical AI technology that is for critical usage, you’re important, you need high reliability and high accuracy. That data that’s used to train it has to be right. And so we don’t hallucinate or the AIs work functionally. So the people who need to train that AI need strong technical skills, but detailed orientation, pattern recognition, puzzle-solving skills. And you need a lot of data to train these AI tools, so you need hyper-focus and a somewhat repetitive task. And years ago, I was doing some research on innovation economies and things like that, and was reading about the Israelis. And almost everyone in Israel does their two years of military service, and the Israelis had soldiers with autism coming in to do their two years, those neurodiverse soldiers. And they built an entire battalion, battalion 9900, which was a cybersecurity battalion because they found these soldiers were extremely adept at going through lines and lines of computer code and finding vulnerabilities, things that needed to be fixed and protect from a cybersecurity standpoint because they had the technical acumen, the detail orientation, the pattern recognition skills, the puzzle solving skills, and the hyperfocus in a competitive task. So data labeling, especially for government and here in the U.S., most data labeling was a huge open field, a green field, because there was no one really doing it. Most data labeling happens overseas at these large sort of like, pay-per-click kind of people doing it at night or in the daytime in China or an internet cafe in the Philippines or in Nepal. And you really can’t take, that’s not a high level of professionalism or technical expertise. And of course, from a security and privacy standpoint from the data, sending stuff overseas is a real issue. So there was no real domestic market or capability to, and certainly not for critical data and classified data to get this data labeled, even though there was demand for AI products and tools and technology. So I thought, well, Here’s an underemployed but highly capable workforce here in the U.S. Data labeling requires technical proficiency, detail orientation, pattern recognition, and puzzle-solving skills. Here’s a U.S. workforce that would do that. And so that’s how we started really focusing on bringing in the neurodiverse workforce and building a company around that.

Terry Gerton A few years ago, the National Geospatial Agency launched a neurodiversity hiring pilot that was based on that same kind of idea that certain intelligence missions align particularly well with strengths like you mentioned, pattern recognition, sustained focus, and attention to detail. Did that help inform your approach? Are you aligned with the NGA initiative in any way?

Peter Kant Well, the NGA initiative actually was based on our work. So yeah, we were aligned. In fact, they hired some of the first people they hired in that initiative were alumni of Enabled Intelligence, but we have a really strong relationship. In fact they’re our largest customer, the NGA is our largest, and we’ve worked together a lot on leverage. In fact we’ve expanded, helped other federal agencies in defense and intelligence expand their neurodiversity programs to leverage these capabilities. We’ve worked with Melwood, which was one of the helpers for the NGA program. They’ve been helpful to us in terms of staffing, identifying people for us to hire. We worked with MITRE, who studied that program at NGA, and we were a party to that as well. So yeah, we have a really strong relationship, And it’s not NGA, I think, was one of the first, but now there is a number of federal agencies really trying to lean in. And leverage the unique skills of this population.

Terry Gerton Peter Kant is the founder and CEO of Enabled Intelligence. Peter, as you speak about the intelligence community, they spend a lot of time recruiting for what seems to be perceived as pretty scarce talent. Based on your experience here and what you’ve seen happen, what would be the most useful changes in the recruiting process that would increase access to and success for this particular talent pool?

Peter Kant What we’ve benefited from and what we’ve built in our recruiting and onboarding and training process to identify and then hopefully, you know, bring aboard and make help our teams be successful is to focus mostly on skills-based and merit-based recruiting, interviewing and assessing of talent. So we’ve built, we know what we want our folks to do, right. There’s an accuracy level, there’s an analytical capability that we’re looking for. So we created as the very first stage, if someone says, hey, I’m interested in working in enabled intelligence, they go through our website and we send them an assessment and they do basically a sample labeling exercise or a data analysis exercise. We have the answer key to that exercise so we can see how well they performed, how quickly they did it, how accurate they are. And at that point, we know they can do the work. Now we’re looking at how do we bring them in? What do they need to be able to be a successful employee here? We’re not looking for cultural fit or did they look us in the eye when they interviewed or here’s the list of you know we it’s a very standard way of a set standard set of questions that we ask. We give those questions ahead of time so there’s no gotchas in terms of we’re not trying to throw someone off their game. We just want if you do the work, that would be great. A lot of talent can be left, if you will, on the cutting room floor if you don’t start with this skills and acumen-based recruiting and assessing versus these other aspects to folks. So that’s been super successful for us. We don’t actively go out and say we want — I mean we do say we’re open to neurodiverse folks but we can’t ask someone if they’re neurodiverse and it’s open to anyone to apply. So by doing this sort of skills-based and acumen-based recruiting and assessing of talent and onboarding of talent We’ve been able to really unlock some of these forgotten avenues or underutilized avenues for talent
